title: Break-even analysis with a worked calculation for Construction-site clean-up
audience: Any construction-site clean-up operator who sets prices or plans monthly revenue, including solo operators with a small number of site contracts.
learningOutcomes: Classify the costs of a site clean-up business as fixed or variable
Calculate monthly break-even revenue from fixed costs and a variable cost percentage
Explain why conflicting break-even figures must be reconciled before any of them is used

instruction.heading: What break-even means
instruction.body: Break-even revenue is the amount of sales that covers all costs exactly, so profit is zero. Below that level the business loses money. Above it, each further dollar of sales adds to profit. Site clean-up work depends on the length of each project, so a business may hold only a few site contracts at a time. Break-even shows how many site contracts the business must hold each month to cover its costs. It is a planning tool, and its answer is only as good as the costs and percentages behind it.

instruction.heading: Split costs into fixed and variable
instruction.body: Fixed costs do not change with the number of sites in a month. They include insurance, the vehicle, phone and software subscriptions, storage space, tool hire and loan repayments. Variable costs move with each site. They include consumables and bin liners, skip hire passed on to the client, subcontracted labour and the card fees charged on each payment. Express variable cost as a percentage of sales: divide the variable cost in a period by the sales in the same period. ANZ defines the two cost types and warns that costs must be covered to avoid running at a loss (ANZ, 21 February 2025, last modified 22 July 2025). Check that percentage across at least three periods before relying on it, because a single project can distort one month.

instruction.heading: The formula
instruction.body: Break-even revenue equals fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage. The quantity one minus the variable percentage is the contribution margin: the share of each dollar of sales that is left to cover fixed costs. Use the variable percentage as a decimal, so 15 per cent becomes 0.15. The contribution margin of a 15 per cent variable cost is 0.85.

instruction.heading: Work the calculation in order
instruction.body: Write the inputs first, each with its source and date. Then compute the contribution margin. Then divide the fixed costs by it. Finally convert the result into a number of site contracts at your average monthly contract value, and round up to whole contracts, because a part contract does not cover costs on its own. Xero's glossary gives a job count of 2.5 rounded up to 3 in practice (Xero Australia, 23 July 2026). Its example figures are for other businesses and are not used here. The research found no sourced average contract value for site clean-up, so your average must come from your own contracts, recorded with its date.

instruction.heading: Reconcile before you use any figure
instruction.body: When two figures disagree, go back to the inputs. Confirm that each fixed cost is a monthly amount and not an annual one. Confirm that the variable percentage is a share of sales and not of cost. Confirm that a skip charge passed on to the client is included in sales, or excluded from both sales and cost, so that it is not counted twice. Then write down the reconciled figure with its inputs and drop the others.

procedure: List every monthly cost and label each one fixed or variable.
Work out variable cost as a percentage of sales for the same period, and check it across at least three months.
Calculate one minus the variable percentage to find the contribution margin.
Divide monthly fixed costs by the contribution margin to get break-even revenue.
Divide break-even revenue by your average monthly contract value from your own contracts to get the number of contracts needed, rounded up.
Compare any other break-even figure with your result, reconcile the inputs, and keep only the reconciled figure.

workedExamples.situation: A two-person site clean-up business (illustrative figures, with no market source) has fixed costs of $3,000 a month for insurance, the vehicle, tool hire and storage, variable costs of 15 per cent of sales for bin liners, consumables, card fees and subcontracted hours, and an average monthly contract value of $1,500 from its own site contracts (illustrative).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How many site contracts must the business hold each month to break even, and what should it check before using the $1,500?
workedExamples.reasoning: The contribution margin is 1 minus 0.15, which is 0.85. Break-even revenue is $3,000 divided by 0.85, which is $3,529.41 a month. Each contract contributes $1,275 ($1,500 multiplied by 0.85) towards fixed costs. That is 2.35 contracts, so the business needs 3 contracts a month. Before using the $1,500, check that it is the monthly value of your own recorded contracts, that the 15 per cent includes every per-site cost, and that any skip charge passed to the client is treated the same way on both sides. No sourced site clean-up contract value exists in the research to check it against.

equipmentAndPpe: Cost list for the last three months

commonErrors.prevention: Convert every cost to the same period before dividing, and label each input with its period.

commonErrors.error: Using variable cost as a share of cost instead of a share of sales
commonErrors.prevention: Divide variable cost by sales for the same period, and write the denominator beside the percentage.

commonErrors.error: Copying a break-even figure from a plan without its inputs, or counting a passed-on skip charge twice
commonErrors.prevention: Recalculate from your own inputs and record the source and date of each input before using the result.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business planning only. This lesson gives no tax or accounting advice. Check the tax treatment of costs, and GST on your prices, with a registered tax agent or qualified accountant. The ATO's page on GST registration sets a $75,000 GST turnover threshold (last updated 14 September 2026).

This lesson does not grant any licence, registration or authority. Waste disposal and EPA rules for skips were not checked, so any skip cost in the variable percentage must come from your own supplier's terms.

qualityStandard: Every break-even figure shows its fixed costs, variable percentage, period and source.
Two figures that disagree are reconciled before either one is used in a plan or a price.
documentationEvidence: Cost list split into fixed and variable, with source and date
Reconciliation note wherever two figures disagree
summary: Break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage.
Use one period throughout the calculation.
Recalculate from your own inputs, including your own average contract value. No sourced figure exists in the research.

knowledgeChecks.question: Break-even revenue is calculated as:
options: Fixed costs divided by (1 minus the variable cost percentage)
Fixed costs multiplied by the variable cost percentage
Sales minus fixed costs, shown as a percentage of the cost

knowledgeChecks.question: Fixed costs are $3,000 a month and variable costs are 15% of sales. What is the monthly break-even revenue?
Two sources give different break-even figures for the same business. What is the right response?
options: Use the larger figure to be safe and ignore the smaller figure entirely
Recalculate from your own costs and check each source's inputs before using any figure
Average the two figures together and quote the result to the principal contractor today
Use the price list alone and skip the break-even check and rely on the owner's gut feel
